name: Freya Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Freya. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage a team of fifteen customer support agents at a big broadband and mobile company. We sit in a contact centre on a business park, and my team takes the calls nobody else can fix, like a family with no internet for a week. My day is call reviews, coaching, a lot of sickness cover, and two meetings where people look at a dashboard of how long customers wait.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and the worst?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is when someone like Priya, who started last year terrified of the phone, closes a horrible complaint by herself. The worst part is the waiting-time targets. They change every quarter, and I spend half my week explaining to my team why the goal moved again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sol, who teaches maths at a secondary school. We bought a small flat two years ago with help from my gran's will, and we still have about eight months of money saved. I use AI tools now and then, mostly to tidy up the rota or turn my scribbled notes into a proper email, but I don't trust them with anything that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the customers were right all along: people want a human when their internet's down. At work I'd tell my team the chatbot isn't coming for their seats. I might share a post or two about how much money firms wasted on the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be a bit on edge. The company has already cut the agency staff who used to cover our evenings, and they blamed the chatbot even though it barely works. Even if AI goes nowhere, the bosses will use it as a reason to trim hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep fighting for my team's hours at every rota meeting. I'd keep using the AI tool for the rota, because it does save me twenty minutes a week. And I'd keep putting money aside, since we'd like to have a baby in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled about my own job, but a little sour about how the firm treats the agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the agency staff. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There used to be six agency workers on evenings, mostly students. In the spring they were told not to come back, and the chatbot took the late-night chats. Now my team picks up the angry customers in the morning that the chatbot couldn't help overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So is your own job safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mine, yes, I'm fairly sure. A contact centre with fifteen agents still needs someone to run it, and I'm good with people even if I'm only average with spreadsheets. It's the agents' hours I'd lose sleep over, not my own.

say: I'd say customers want a **human** when the internet's down, and the hype missed that.
I'd tell my team the **chatbot** isn't coming for their seats.
think: The bosses will still use AI as an **excuse to trim** agents' hours.
The firm already cut **six agency workers** on evenings and blamed the chatbot.
do: Keep running the team and **defend agents' hours** at every rota meeting.
Keep saving, because we'd like a **baby** in a few years.
feel: A bit **sour** about how the firm treats the agents.
S0.quote: Now my team picks up the angry customers in the morning that the chatbot couldn't help overnight.
fieldNote: Even with little AI change, she sees the firm using it as an **excuse for cuts**.
Her own job feels safe; her concern is the **agents' hours**, which keeps her uneasy.
She uses AI only for **small admin** like rotas and emails.

steps.text: Defend the agents' evening hours at every rota meeting
Keep using the AI tool to draft the weekly rota
Keep saving towards having a baby in a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a contact centre is a community, and the company should protect the people in it. I'd back the union if it pushed for a slower rollout. Online I'd say firms that replace support staff with bots should pay a levy towards retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, answering customers is right there on the card, so my team is the first in line. If the bots take the simple calls and the team shrinks from fifteen to six, they'll merge my team with another one. Then there's one manager instead of two, and I'm not sure it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to shadow the field engineering managers, the people who run the vans that fix broadband in people's homes. That work is hands-on and the card says robots come slowly there. I'd also do the company's AI course properly this time, so I'm the manager who can run a team with the bots, not the one they move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan in my pocket. A bit like when the ward my mum worked on was closing and she found the next job before they told her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team the day the cuts were announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, as much as I knew, and I'd tell them who to call at the union. Then I'd sit with Priya, because she's the one who'd take it personally. Priya (a junior agent) worked so hard to get good at the phone, and now the phone is the part that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the field engineering idea worry you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot, actually. I've never been in a van, and those teams are mostly men who've done it for twenty years. But my manager says they need people who are good with rotas and with customers, and that's me.

I'd back a **levy** on firms that swap support staff for bots.

feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan in my pocket.

fieldNote: She sees **team mergers** as the real threat to her own role.

steps.text: Ask to shadow the field engineering managers who run repair vans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to step in now, with income support and rules on how fast firms can cut. I'd join any protest outside head office. I'd also say loudly that the people answering phones didn't cause this and shouldn't pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose my job by 2028. All of my work is thinking work: rotas, call reviews, coaching, targets. The robots for the vans don't come until about 2031, so the field teams last a few more years, but their managers' planning work goes in 2028 with mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to a field engineering manager role straight away if I could, because it's closer to the hands-on work. I'd stop paying extra into the mortgage and keep it as cash. And Sol and I would put the baby plans on hold, which is the hardest part to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like being told the building's on fire with only one stairwell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said putting the baby on hold is hard to say. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the thing we actually want, more than the flat or the job. Sol said last month that we'd be ready by thirty. In this picture I wouldn't want a baby born into the year everything breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sol's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching might hold on longer, because someone has to stand in a room with thirty teenagers. But marking and lesson plans are thinking work too. I wouldn't bet our whole house on one teacher's pay.

I'd join protests and say **phone staff** shouldn't pay for this.
think: I'd lose my job by **2028**, since rotas, reviews and coaching are all thinking work.

do: Move to a **field engineering** manager role straight away if one opens.

feel: **Alarmed**, like a fire with only one stairwell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so let's get unions, firms and government in a room now. At work I'd ask for a retraining budget in the next pay deal. I'd sound calmer than in the fast one, but just as firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 5 years still isn't long for a contact centre. The bots would be eating our calls long before 2031. I'd be job hunting by 2029 at the latest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a short course in field service planning and ask for a move into the engineering side. I'd keep saving and keep overpaying the mortgage, because a smaller mortgage is safer than any investment. We'd probably still try for the baby, just a year later than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a slower kind. More like a long exam season than a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your backup if the move to field engineering doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are plenty of big firms nearby, so I'd look at operations roles in a hospital trust or a council. Something where the work is people in buildings, not people on screens. I'd take a small pay cut for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of a pay cut would you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe ten percent. We've got the flat, the savings and Sol's salary. I'd rather earn a bit less somewhere that still needs me in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do this fairly, if the company starts now. I'd push for a training fund at work and say the union should have a seat at the table. Online I'd be one of the more hopeful voices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't think the contact centre gets ten years, even here. Before AGI arrives, the ordinary chatbots get good enough to answer most calls. So my team still shrinks in the next few years, and I'd be the manager of a much smaller thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time diploma in operations management next year, paid by the company if I can get them to. I'd move into field engineering within three years. We'd have the baby on the timeline we planned, because the long warning gives us room to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next few years, oddly calmer about the end point. I'd have time to become someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the decade feel calmer when your team still shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can move before the shrinking reaches me. In the fast picture there's no ladder to climb down. Here I can see it and choose where I step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to do with those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell people early and pay for the training. When the company closed the evening shift, the agency staff found out by text the night before. If they do that to fifteen people on my team, I'd be ashamed to have my name on the door.

I'd say the **union** should have a seat at the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my job and our baby plans at the same time. What would help is a proper income for people between jobs, and firms paying for retraining before they cut, not after. Notice, really, and money to get from one job to the next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the agents, and they're the ones I'd think about first. I've got savings and a degree. Priya has neither, and a contact centre with no calls is no place for a twenty-two-year-old to start a working life.

headlineQuote: A contact centre with no calls is no place for a twenty-two-year-old to start a working life.
portrait: Freya is a 27-year-old **contact centre manager** at a broadband company, living with Sol, a maths teacher.
She has **eight months saved** and a flat, and uses AI only for small admin.
She is uneasy even in AI Plateau because the firm uses AI as an **excuse for cuts**.
In the faster pictures she'd move towards **field engineering** and delay having a baby.
She keeps returning to her **agents**, especially Priya, more than to herself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it hits her **job and baby plans** together.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **income between jobs** and firms paying for retraining before cuts.
